text:
**Yes, a cable can limit charging speed, but only when its rating is lower than what your charger and device would otherwise negotiate.** The charger and device agree on a power level, and the cable caps it. USB-IF notes that a certified cable doesn't augment the capabilities of the products it connects ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)).

**What the ratings mean**
- **60W:** 20V at 3A. This is enough for phones, tablets, and many smaller laptops.
- **100W:** 20V at 5A, which requires an e-marker chip in the cable. The UL article says 100W cables were replaced in the spec by 240W ones ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations)). USB-IF stopped certifying 100W cables on December 22, 2021 ([USB-IF](https://compliance.usb.org/index.asp?Format=Standard&UpdateFile=Cables+and+Connectors&pubDate=20261005)). So you'll still find 100W cables on the market, but newly certified cables are labeled only 60W or 240W.
- **240W:** 48V at 5A, called Extended Power Range (EPR). It requires an e-marker, and USB PD 3.1 adds the 28V, 36V, and 48V steps that give 140W, 180W, and 240W ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)).

**Which cable you need**
- **Device charges at 60W or less (phones, tablets, most small laptops):** a 60W cable won't slow you down.
- **Device wants 65–100W (many laptops):** use a 5A, e-marked cable. A 60W cable will cap you at about 60W.
- **Device and charger both support more than 100W:** you need a 240W cable.

**How to check yours:** look for a 60W or 240W logo on the cable or its packaging. USB-IF requires this marking on certified USB-C to USB-C cables ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)). Unmarked cables are usually safest treated as 60W or lower.

**Two caveats**
- Charging speed is also limited by the charger and the device. A 240W cable won't make a 30W charger faster.
- Power rating and data speed are separate. Some 100W or 240W cables are USB 2.0 only (480 Mbps), so they charge fast but transfer data slowly and can't carry video.

**If you need a 100W cable:** the [Baseus USB-C to USB-C Cable, 100W](https://dealectric.com/go/baseus-usb-c-cable-100w) is listed at $9.99 for 1 m (Dealectric, verified 2026-10-21). It is 5A and e-marked but USB 2.0 only, has no video output, and isn't rated for 140W/240W. Baseus also notes it isn't supported for iPad Pro charging ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/baseus-usb-c-cable-100w)). That link is an affiliate link, so Dealectric earns a commission if you buy through it. It also hasn't gone through the newer USB-IF 60W/240W labeling, so I can't say it's certified.

If you tell me your charger and device (or laptop model), I can say which rating you need.
